analysis.one_liner: Bans minors from dangerous jobs and sharply raises penalties for companies using child labor.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote: it sat in two House committees from October 2023 until the Congress ended with 22 cosponsors, all Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strengthen federal child labor rules by automatically classifying workers under 18 in meat processing, manufacturing, mining, demolition, and explosives work as illegal child labor, and would require the Labor Department to regularly update the list of jobs too dangerous for minors. It would make companies responsible for child labor anywhere in their supply chains, let the government freeze work sites that employ children illegally, and raise civil penalties to as much as $690,000 per violation (double for repeat or willful violations), with new compensatory and punitive damages for child workers who are hurt. It would also apply stricter child labor rules to federal contractors and require annual reports on work-related injuries and deaths.
analysis.who_benefits: Minors, especially teenagers and migrant children working in meatpacking plants, factories, agriculture supply chains, and construction, who would gain stronger protections, higher employer penalties for violations, and a private right to damages. The Labor Department would gain new enforcement tools, and federal taxpayers would gain assurance that government contracts are performed without child labor.

how_it_helps.text: Under current law, 16- and 17-year-olds can legally work in many hazardous jobs; the bill would make it illegal child labor for anyone under 18 to work in manufacturing, mining, trenching or excavation, meat processing, demolition, or with explosives [S2].

The Labor Department would have to issue updated hazard rules within 180 days and revisit them at least every five years, closing a gap where the list of banned dangerous jobs had not kept pace with new industries [S2].

Companies would be barred from selling goods produced with child labor by their contractors or subcontractors at any tier, and could keep 'hot goods' off shipment for 180 days; the bill also allows the government to affix 'Unlawfully manufactured; child labor' tags to violating goods [S2].
The Secretary of Labor could issue stop-work orders against violators, and employers would have to pay workers whose jobs were halted by such an order [S2].

Civil penalties would rise to $151,380 per child employed, and $690,000 for violations causing death or serious injury, each doubleable for willful or repeat violations; criminal fines would rise to $750,000 [S2].

Child workers who were victims of violations could recover at least $75,000 in compensatory damages, or at least $750,000 where a violation causes death or serious injury, plus possible punitive damages of at least $1 million, and would have 10 years to sue [S2].
Federal contracts and Davis-Bacon or Service Contract Act work would carry a no-child-labor requirement at every subcontract tier, with a three-year ban on new federal contracts for violators [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Industries that employ minors in low-wage, high-hazard work — meat processing, food and agriculture supply chains, manufacturing, and construction contractors — would face higher compliance costs, much larger fines when children are used illegally, joint liability across their supply chains for subcontractor violations, and potential three-year exclusion from federal contracting.
analysis.who_pays_short: Meat processors, manufacturers, and federal contractors

drawbacks.text: The bill's supply-chain liability and successor-in-interest rules would make large companies financially responsible for violations by small subcontractors they may not control, and the good-faith defense requires documented 'meaningful and affirmative' auditing steps — a compliance burden that would fall hardest on smaller firms [S2].

The fixed penalty and damages floors ($75,000 per affected employee, up to $690,000 civil and $750,000 criminal per violation) are severe enough that an honest supporter would acknowledge they could push some low-margin employers to avoid hiring even legal teen workers rather than risk liability [S2].

Because the bill defines the entire 'place of work' as covered and lets the Secretary add occupations by order, the practical effect could restrict legitimate work opportunities for older teens in industries adjacent to the banned list [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections are well-targeted at a documented problem: minors, including migrant children, found working in meatpacking and other hazardous jobs, under an enforcement system with penalties too small to deter violations. The costs are real but are the costs of serious enforcement — higher compliance burdens and stiffer fines. The main design risk is that broad supply-chain liability may land on companies far removed from the actual violation, though the bill includes a good-faith defense for contractors that audited their suppliers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to two House committees in October 2023, and neither committee ever took it up, so it died there when the term ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the Children Harmed In Life-threatening or Dangerous Labor Act (CHILD Labor Act) on October 26, 2023, with ten original cosponsors [S2, S4].

The same day, the House referred the bill to the Education and Workforce Committee and the Oversight and Accountability Committee; the Speaker splits first referrals among committees by jurisdiction [S4].
Twenty-two House members cosponsored the bill, all Democrats; no Republicans cosponsored it [S3].
The action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action after the initial referral — the bill remained in committee through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers in industries that hire minors in hazardous work — meat and food processing, manufacturing, agriculture supply chains, and construction contractors — are better off, since they face no new penalties, supply-chain liability, or stop-work orders. The current low penalties for child labor violations remain in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who use hazardous child labor

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely partisan: all 22 cosponsors were Democrats, no Republican signed on, and the Republican-run committees that held the bill took no action.

industries.note: The bill would make it illegal child labor for anyone under 18 to work in meat processing and would raise penalties for violations to as much as $690,000 per child, doubleable. The industry has employed underage workers in recent years, and the current small fines are the reason enforcement rarely deters it.

Minors would be barred outright from manufacturing and mining work, with updated hazard orders every five years. Manufacturers using subcontractor labor would also bear liability for child labor anywhere in their supply chains.

Davis-Bacon, Service Contract Act, and Walsh-Healey contracts would carry child labor bans at every subcontract tier, with liquidated damages, contract cancellation, and a three-year ban on new federal contracts for violators.

The bill exempts a parent employing their own child but holds food brands responsible for goods produced with child labor by their suppliers, with 'hot goods' shipment restrictions and child labor tags. Compliant producers gain a more level field against violators using cheap underage labor.
